title: Language Sample Analysis Practices in a Multilingual and Diglossic Context: A Survey of Speech-Language Pathologists in German-Speaking Switzerland
abstract: Purpose: This study investigated the frequency, purpose, target groups, and methods of language sample analysis (LSA) among speech-language pathologists (SLPs) in German-speaking Switzerland. LSA is particularly relevant in linguistically diverse and underresearched contexts such as diglossic settings, where everyday spoken language differs from standardized varieties. Method: A survey was conducted among 550 SLPs in German-speaking Switzerland. Descriptive statistics were used to analyze the data, focusing on reported use, target demographics, and analytical methods concerning LSA. Results: Compared with previous research from English-speaking countries, LSA is used by a larger proportion of SLPs in Switzerland. Consistent with prior findings, Swiss SLPs primarily employ individualized approaches rather than established protocols. LSA is most frequently conducted in younger children, while the use of assistive tools remains low. Furthermore, SLPs mainly focus on microstructural parameters (e.g., morphology–syntax) rather than on macrostructural parameters during analysis. Conclusions: The LSA is a highly utilized method in German-speaking Switzerland, underscoring its clinical rel

title: Effects of Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Intervention Strategies and Visual Scene Displays on Autistic Children's Joint Engagement
abstract: Purpose: Naturalistic developmental behavioral intervention (NDBI) and visual scene displays (VSDs), a type of augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), are research-supported practices focused on naturalistic instruction and increasing social communication skills in young autistic children. The purpose of our study was to extend previous research to understand the effects of embedding VSDs within a dynamic play-based NDBI for young autistic children. Method: We employed a randomized multiple-baseline single-case experimental design across three participants to evaluate the effects of (a) NDBI strategies and (b) NDBI strategies plus aided AAC modeling and just-in-time (JIT) programming of VSDs on joint engagement in young autistic children. Results: When NDBI strategies were introduced, there was a large positive effect on child joint engagement and a corresponding large negative effect on child isolated attention. After aided AAC modeling and JIT programming were introduced, child joint engagement and isolated attention outcomes were mixed. Conclusions: The findings of the current study show promise to using VSDs within dynamic play-based NDBIs as a communication support.

title: Investigating Variability and Malleability of Speech-Language Pathologists' Responsive Talk With Children: An Early-Efficacy Trial
abstract: Purpose: The purposes of this early-stage efficacy study were to examine speech-language pathologists' (SLPs') use of responsive talk with children and to determine the extent to which responsive talk can be modified through brief clinician education or an in situ, tablet-based feedback system, GENIE, that provided real-time prompts to use responsive talk. Method: Eleven SLPs (certified clinicians and graduate students) and 11 typically developing preschool-aged children participated in a quasi-experimental study. SLPs were paired with a randomly assigned child to complete two structured intervention sessions to assess responsive talk. In the first session, SLPs used their business-as-usual practices, whereas in the second session, SLPs were randomly assigned to receive clinician education or the in situ GENIE prompts, representing a planned variation in instructing SLPs to use responsive talk during intervention. SLP responsive talk was coded from video-recorded interactions to establish the frequency of use. Results: SLPs demonstrated substantial variability in the baseline use of responsive talk. title: Communication Difficulties and Management: The Lived Experience of Individuals With Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration Spectrum Disorders
abstract: Purpose: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) is the neuropathology that underlies a collection of progressive clinical syndromes typically classified by the initial/primary symptom. For example, individuals with loss of word meaning as a first manifestation are often diagnosed with the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia. Growing evidence suggests that language and communication can be impacted in all clinical syndromes across the FTLD spectrum, but the functional relevance of these symptoms has yet to be explored. Method: The Frontotemporal Degeneration (FTD) Insights Survey is the largest community survey of individuals affected by FTLD. It was administered online and included questions related to demographics, symptoms, life participation, quality of life, and experiences with and hopes for treatment. Self-reported diagnoses of respondents included the nonfluent/agrammatic, semantic, and unspecified variants of primary progressive aphasia, semantic dementia, corticobasal syndrome, progressive supranuclear palsy, and behavioral variant FTD. title: Core Lexicon Analysis of a Storytelling Task in Korean-Speaking Individuals With Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to validate newly developed, age-stratified Korean core lexicon (CL) checklists and evaluate their clinical utility in assessing discourse production in persons with aphasia (PWA) using a culturally familiar storytelling task. Method: Thirty-six PWA and 36 age- and education-matched cognitively healthy adults (CHAs) participated in a Korean picture-based storytelling task. Percentage of core nouns and verbs were calculated using age-specific checklists and compared across group (CHAs vs. PWA) and lexical category (noun vs. verb). We also examined whether core noun and verb percentages were associated with aphasia severity and which word class significantly predicted severity. Results: PWA exhibited significantly lower percentage of CL than CHAs, with a larger noun–verb difference observed in PWA than in CHAs. Pearson correlation analyses showed that both core nouns and verbs were significantly and positively associated with aphasia severity. title: Pushing the Limits on Learning Gender-Affirming Voice: An Autoethnography From a Client
abstract: Gender-affirming voice work differs fundamentally from other speech-language pathology work. Rather than addressing pathology in communication, gender-affirming voice work teaches clients how to change behavior, which is limited in part by how gender-diverse people interact with their social environment. Integrating my original theory of gender with my personal experience learning gender-affirming voice, I explain possible obstacles gender-diverse people face as well as recommendations to speech-language pathologists to mitigate them. In particular, gender-diverse people may exhibit difficulties in auditory processing, vocal biomechanics, and generalization into gender expression. However, despite unique challenges presented by gender-affirming voice work, my experience is overall positive and worth the effort.

title: The Management of Swallowing Disorders in Children With Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type 1: A Scoping Review
abstract: Purpose: Spinal muscular atrophy Type 1 (SMA1) is a rare autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder with progressive muscle weakness and atrophy. Dysphagia is common among children with SMA1, and its complications are frequently documented. This scoping review aimed to describe the management of swallowing disorders in this population. Method: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, four electronic databases were searched (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane Library) for studies on children with SMA1. We investigated the management of swallowing disorders in children with SMA1, including methods and protocols used to assess swallowing and feeding, and treatment option. The quality of included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklists; two independent researchers conducted study selection and data extraction. Results: Thirty-eight studies with a total of 1,784 SMA1 patients were included. Swallowing was evaluated using instrumental methods (flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing and videofluoroscopic swallowing study) and clinical assessments, with one validated protocol identified for pediatric SMA

title: Variety Matters: Measuring Semantic Verb Types in Conversation Following ECoLoGiC Treatment for People With Moderate or Severe Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: Expanding Communication and Language Opportunities Generated in Conversation Treatment (ECoLoGiC-Tx) is a conversation treatment designed to improve the everyday language abilities of people with moderate-to-severe aphasia. Previous research reported improved use of basic syntactic structures during posttreatment conversations. Although ECoLoGic-Tx does not specifically target verb use, it may change the frequency and/or types of verbs used during conversation. Semantic verb type analysis categorizes verbs by their intended meaning. Each of the five semantic verb types serves a unique function during discourse, and difficulty using verbs within and across semantic categories may limit what is shared during everyday interactions. Because verbs play an essential role in conversation, this study explores if ECoLoGiC-Tx changed the frequency and semantic categories of verbs used by people with aphasia (PWA). Method: Ten PWA attended 60-min treatment sessions twice weekly for 10 weeks. Conversational discourse samples were collected three times at each assessment phase (pretreatment, posttreatment, and maintenance). Samples were analyzed for overall verb frequency and semantic

title: Feasibility and Efficacy of a Hybrid Delivery Model of the Categorization Program for Individuals With Chronic Traumatic Brain Injury: A Pilot Study
abstract: Purpose: The present study examined the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a hybrid, telehealth-adapted delivery of the Categorization Program (CP), an evidence-based cognitive rehabilitation intervention, for adults with chronic moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (msTBI) who were living in the community and not engaged in ongoing rehabilitation services. It was hypothesized that the telehealth-adapted CP would demonstrate high feasibility and lead to improvements in intervention-specific and standardized neuropsychological outcomes. Method: This study employed a single-group, pre–post intervention design with follow-up assessments. Adults aged 18–65 years with msTBI sustained at least 1 year prior to enrollment were recruited from hospital and rehabilitation center databases. Participants completed a baseline neuropsychological assessment, followed by the eight-level, hierarchically structured CP intervention delivered primarily via telehealth. Neuropsychological measures were administered pre-intervention and post-intervention, while CP-specific measures were administered pre-intervention and post-intervention and at 4- and 8-week follow-ups. Feasibility was evaluated

title: Applying the Social Communication Implementable and Applicable Lens Framework to Intervention
abstract: Purpose: The Social Communication Implementable and Applicable Lens (SoCIAL) is a framework that offers a comprehensive, context-sensitive approach to the assessment and intervention of social communication for individuals with brain injury. Building upon foundational models such as the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, the Model of Cognitive-Communication Competence, and the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System, SoCIAL emphasizes the interplay of identity, skills, demands, and environment in shaping communicative participation and quality of life. This clinical focus article demonstrates the application of the SoCIAL framework to evidence-based intervention to support holistic, person-centered care. Through a detailed clinical case study, we illustrate how intervention targets and ingredients, collaborative goal setting, and contextual flexibility can be addressed in the context of the framework. Conclusion: The framework's alignment with current literature and guidelines underscores its utility in guiding clinicians to design, implement, and measure evidence-based social communication interventions that develop skills, support meaningful

title: Priorities and Fractures in DeafPlus Augmentative and Alternative Communication Decision-Making Teams
abstract: Purpose: Children who are DeafPlus often engage in multiple services across a range of settings. For children who are DeafPlus using augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), decisions require further distributed expertise when communication planning. However, the processes that these teams engage in when decision making for this cohort remains underexamined. Method: This qualitative study analyzed the transcripts of three focus groups to gain insight into how professionals perceive and experience aspects of multidisciplinary interaction such as negotiating roles, authority, and communication approaches specifically for students who are DeafPlus using AAC. Results: Within these teams and their decision-making processes, data revealed the presence of (a) unclear and overlapping roles, (b) conflicting perspectives on communication modalities, (c) gatekeeping and power in support team participation, (d) fragmented and inconsistent processes, and (e) system constraints shaping decisions. title: The Relationship Between Dynamic Assessment of Analogical Reasoning and Syntax in French-Speaking Children With and Without Developmental Language Disorder
abstract: Purpose: According to usage-based theories of language development, typically developing (TD) children rely on analogical reasoning (AR) to learn syntactic structures. However, children with developmental language disorder (DLD) demonstrate difficulties in AR, which could contribute to explaining their difficulties in acquiring syntactic structures. While previous studies have reported no link between nonverbal AR and syntax using static assessment, we shifted focus onto dynamic assessment to explore the relationship between these two domains' learning potential in a French-speaking population. Method: Ninety-seven TD children (25 bilingual) and 98 children with DLD (40 bilingual; M age = 8;8 [years;months]) were assessed by using (a) a static task of AR; (b) a static task of syntax; (c) a dynamic task of AR, with prompts assisting the learner to analyze the analogy required to complete the matrix; and (d) a dynamic task of syntax targeting six structures, with prompts based on syntactic priming. Results: Children with DLD scored lower than TD children on all our measures, except when considering the progression within the dynamic task of AR, where children improved similarly. Stat

title: Service Delivery Barriers in Pediatric Feeding Disorder: A Path Forward
abstract: Purpose: This article examines barriers and facilitators to the care of children with pediatric feeding disorder (PFD), a complex condition that impacts individuals, families, medical institutions, and communities. Method: This clinical focus article was developed through a targeted literature synthesis and conceptual analysis leading to the identification and grouping of care barriers. Results: Multiple barriers affecting professionals and caregivers were identified, including limitations in resources, clinical tools, care coordination, accessibility, and caregiver-related factors. Conclusions: The identification of barriers reveals the need for unified strategic approaches to improve care efforts. Five key initiatives are proposed: advancing research, policy, and guidelines; providing PFD-specific professional training; expanding access to care; strengthening support systems; and enhancing caregiver education and engagement.

title: What Temperament Can Tell Us About Language Development of Late-Talking Toddlers
abstract: Purpose: The primary aim of this study was to compare temperamental traits in typically developing and late-talking toddlers. A secondary aim was to evaluate potential associations between language skills and temperament within each group. Method: Caregivers of typically developing ( n = 21) and late-talking ( n = 21) toddlers, aged 18–35 months, completed a brief measure of temperament (Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire–Very Short Form) and expressive vocabulary (MacArthur–Bates Communicative Development Inventories: Words and Sentences). Toddlers' expressive and receptive language skills were also directly assessed using the Mullen Scales of Early Learning. Results: There were no significant group differences on the temperament measurement between general constructs; however, late talkers showed lower levels of sensory discomfort and positive anticipation compared to typical talkers. Associations between language and temperament differed between groups. For typical talkers, larger vocabularies were associated with higher levels of positive emotions and sociability. title: Craniofacial Education in Accredited Graduate Speech-Language Pathology Programs: National Patterns in Coursework and Clinical Training
abstract: Purpose: This study provides an updated national examination of craniofacial education across accredited graduate speech-language pathology programs in the United States. Method: A survey was distributed to 289 accredited graduate speech-language pathology programs. Ninety-nine programs completed all or part of the survey. Publicly available curricular materials were reviewed for nonresponding programs, and brief follow-up correspondence was conducted when necessary. The final data set included 281 programs. Data were analyzed descriptively to characterize coursework structure and clinical training opportunities. Results: Among the 281 programs analyzed, 19.9% offered a dedicated and required craniofacial course and 11.4% offered a dedicated elective course. The majority of programs (68.7%) reported covering craniofacial content exclusively through embedded instruction. Sixty-three percent of programs reported offering clinical experiences involving individuals with craniofacial conditions, although most indicated that fewer than 25% of students engaged in these experiences. title: Screening Beyond First Words: A Scoping Review of Speech and Language Screening Tools and Approaches for 2- and 3-Year-Olds
abstract: Purpose: The task of being able to accurately and efficiently identify children in the early years at risk of future speech sound and/or language disorders remains elusive. To progress toward more accurate identification, the breadth of skills examined in current screening tools and approaches needs to be determined. Our purpose was to (a) understand the key characteristics of screening tools and approaches for children aged 2–3 years, (b) determine the psychometric quality of screening tools and approaches, and (c) identify the early years health and education professionals who screen toddlers' speech and language skills. Method: A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) methodological framework and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension guidelines. A systematic search of the literature was conducted, and the data were described through data extraction, quality appraisal, percentage and frequency counts, and a narrative synthesis. title: Comparing Emotional Facial Expressions Produced During Personal Narrative Discourse by People With and Without Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: This preliminary study aimed to (a) determine whether the frequency and intensity of emotional facial expressions during personal narrative discourse are different for people with aphasia (PWA) than for adults without aphasia and (b) explore the relationship between the frequency and intensity of emotional facial expressions and aphasia severity. Method: Fifty-two participants, including 26 PWA and 26 control participants, were randomly selected from Aphasia Bank, a protocoled database with video recordings of both people with and without aphasia. Two video-recorded narrative discourse samples, a stroke/illness story and an important life event story, from each participant were used. Two human coders were trained utilizing a modified Facial Expression Coding System to identify emotional facial expressions according to valence (positive/negative) and intensity (perceptual scale from 1 to 4). Dependent variables included the frequency and intensity of positive and negative facial expressions. title: The Effects of Immersive Virtual Reality on Discourse Production in Younger and Older Adults
abstract: Purpose: Discourse production tasks are widely used to assess language across clinical and research contexts. Virtual reality (VR) offers an alternative discourse elicitation modality by providing immersive 3-D environments that may influence language production differently from traditional picture-based tasks. This study examined whether immersive VR affects discourse production compared with traditional picture description tasks as well as how younger and older adults perceive the usability and acceptability of and relative preference for each modality. Method: Forty-five younger and 33 older neurotypical adults described two widely studied images (Cookie Theft and Cat Rescue), presented either as colored 2-D images or as immersive 3-D VR environments. Participants completed both modalities in a counterbalanced order and completed a posttask VR usability survey. Discourse samples were analyzed for total utterances, total words, mean length of utterance (MLU), proportion of open- and closed-class words, moving-average type–token ratio (MATTR), and embedded clauses. title: Evaluating Intrarater Reliability of Nasopharyngoscopy Ratings Made by Speech-Language Pathologists in a Clinical Versus Research Setting
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to evaluate intrarater reliability for nasopharyngoscopy ratings of velopharyngeal closure across two contexts: ratings made in a clinical setting and ratings made in a research setting using standardized rating definitions. Method: Five speech-language pathologists participated in this study. Two assessments of intrarater reliability were performed: between ratings from clinical reports and re-ratings made in a research setting and videos re-rated twice in a research setting. Nasopharyngoscopy ratings analyzed included velopharyngeal closure pattern, total percent closure, and extent of velar movement. Reliability was calculated using Cohen's kappa and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Results: Intrarater reliability between clinical reports and re-ratings made in a research setting varied for closure pattern from weak ( k = .24) to perfect ( k = 1.00), for total percent closure from poor (ICC = −.09) to good (ICC = .81), and for extent of velar movement from moderate (ICC = .57) to good (ICC = .80). title: Preliminary Evidence for the Effects of Bilingual ECoLoGiC Treatment for People With Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: The focus of this preliminary study is to report the effects of bilingual Expanding Communication and Language Opportunities Generated in Conversation Treatment (ECoLoGiC-Tx) on formal measures of language, functional communication, and patient/family-reported outcomes (P/FROMs) in bilingual people with aphasia (PWA). Method: Two bilingual participants, P1 (70 years old, Hebrew–English, moderate Broca's aphasia) and P2 (73 years old, Yiddish–English, mild anomic aphasia), participated in this quasi-experimental, pretest/posttest case series, with a follow-up session 6 weeks after the bilingual intervention. The use of the ECoLoGiC-Tx model for bilingual PWA incorporated dual-language use, including code-switching, translanguaging, and translation, as natural communicative choices. Therapy was personalized and context sensitive, taking into account each participant's sociocultural and linguistic history, language preferences, and real-life communication contexts, with an emphasis on person-centered goals and participant-driven meaningful conversation. title: Communication Changes Following SPEAK OUT!: Perspectives of People With Parkinson's Disease and Their Care Partners
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to examine whether the SPEAK OUT!® Therapy Program impacts patient self-reported outcomes in communicative effectiveness and voice function for people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and hypokinetic dysarthria and to identify patient factors (e.g., cognition, dysarthria severity) that influence treatment response. In addition, we examined how care partners perceived changes in PwPD's communicative effectiveness following SPEAK OUT! and how self-ratings and care partner ratings compared to each other. Method: Twenty-seven PwPD completed the SPEAK OUT! Therapy Program via telehealth. Two patient-reported outcome measures (i.e., Communication Effectiveness Survey [CES] and Voice Handicap Index-10 [VHI-10]) were collected at three pretreatment and three posttreatment timepoints. A subset of 13 PwPD had care partners who also provided CES ratings at pre- and posttreatment timepoints. title: Analysis of Speech-Language Pathologist and Preprofessional Student Observations of Parent–Child Play Interactions
abstract: Purpose: Initial clinical observations help establish a strengths-based caregiver coaching relationship and guide intervention planning. This study examined what caregiver–child communication strategies speech-language pathologists (SLPs) and master's-level graduate students prioritize when making an initial observation of a naturalistic play interaction. Method: Twenty American Speech-Language-Hearing Association–certified SLPs and 20 master's-level graduate students reviewed videos of caregiver–child play interactions and answered open-ended questions related to what they observed in the interactions. Responses were analyzed using directed content analysis focused on strategies related to environmental arrangement and language facilitation relevant to language development. Results: Across 1,469 coded thought units, participants' comments centered on teachable caregiver actions (facilitation strategies) more than environmental features. There were minimal differences in the quality of comments made by SLPs and graduate students. title: Exploring the Self-Perceived Role of South African Speech-Language Pathologists in Youth Correctional Facilities
abstract: Purpose: Justice-involved youth (JIY) represent a vulnerable population with a well-documented elevated risk for language disorder compared to their nonoffending peers. Research also suggests that JIY with language disorder are more likely to reoffend after release. Despite this, the involvement of speech-language pathologists (SLPs) in JIY rehabilitation in South Africa remains limited. This study explored the perceptions of South African SLPs regarding their potential roles in youth correctional facilities. Method: A cross-sectional, mixed-method online survey design was used. Participants were recruited by means of nonprobability purposive sampling through various social media platforms. A total of 35 complete data sets were collected. Results: Most participants were unfamiliar with the current role of SLPs in youth correctional facilities ( n = 25, 86.2%). Despite this, most viewed SLP involvement as potentially beneficial to JIY rehabilitation ( n = 26, 74.3%) and agreed with the need for increased advocacy for the involvement of SLPs in JIY rehabilitation programs ( n = 23, 79.3%), although fewer than half reported feeling comfortable working in youth correctional settings (

title: Effectiveness of an Online Perceptual Evaluation of Voice Training Platform on the Rater Reliability in Novice Raters
abstract: Purpose: The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of an online perceptual evaluation of voice training platform in improving the rater reliability of novice raters. The secondary aim was to determine the relationship between the training duration and rating accuracy. Method: Forty-two speech-language pathology students participated in this study. Training was conducted using an online training platform over a 12-week period. The online training platform was developed based on perceptual learning theory and includes three main components: (a) familiarization with vocal parameters, (b) training with a single vocal parameter, and (c) training with multiple vocal parameters. Students were instructed to use the training platform to practice auditory–perceptual ratings both inside and outside the classroom. All voice samples included three vocal tasks: sustained vowels, passage reading, and conversational speech. Results: Intrarater exact agreement showed statistically significant improvements after training. title: Engaging Children in Brain–Computer Interface (BCI) Development: Utilizing an Interactive iPad Tool to Capture Picture-Based P300-Based BCI Augmentative and Alternative Communication Design Preferences
abstract: Introduction: P300-based brain–computer interface augmentative and alternative communication (P300-BCI-AAC) systems show promise for supporting communication for children with severe speech and physical impairments. However, little is known about how children prefer these displays to be designed. This study examined children's design choices and the rationales guiding those choices to inform the development of user-centered, pediatric BCI-AAC displays. Method: Thirty-eight typically developing children (8–12 years of age) used a P300-BCI-AAC design application to create their preferred picture-based interface. Participants selected features such as color, animation, and overlays. Semistructured interviews followed to capture reasons for their decisions. Results: Two themes guided design decisions: (a) supporting visual distinction to make items more recognizable and (b) personal factors influencing design choices. Most children selected preferred colors; animation effects, especially zooming animations; and sound cues. title: Social Disadvantage and Language Disorder: Is Dissociating Possible?
abstract: Purpose: We (a) investigated whether children of lower socioeconomic status (SES) are at a greater risk of developmental language disorder (DLD) than children of higher SES, based on standardized assessment; (b) identified the language skills most strongly affected by SES; and (c) examined which standardized and naturalistic measures best differentiate DLD in children from lower SES backgrounds. Method: We compared Russian-speaking children of middle SES (urban) and low SES (rural) on standardized language tasks. To disentangle SES effects from heritable risk for DLD, we further compared low-SES children from two rural populations—one with a high prevalence of DLD and one with an average level of DLD—using standardized language tasks and indices of narrative microstructure. Results: Rural children performed more poorly than urban children across all assessments, whereas the two rural samples differed only minimally on most subtests. Sentence repetition showed the largest SES effect and the smallest DLD effect. title: A Qualitative Evidence Synthesis of Communication Partner Training: Exploring the Experiences of Communication Partners and People With Acquired Brain Injury
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to explore the experiences of adult communication partners (CPs) of individuals with acquired brain injury (ABI) who received communication training and, where reported, the experiences of individuals with ABI who attended or participated in the training. Method: A qualitative evidence synthesis was conducted. Electronic searches were completed in CINAHL Ultimate, APA PsycInfo, APA PsycArticles, Medline, Embase, AMED, Scopus, NeuroBITE, and PubMed for studies published until August 2025. Included studies described an intervention directed at adult CPs where the program focus was on improving communicative participation for adults post-ABI. Relevant data were extracted and inductively synthesized using thematic synthesis. Studies were appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme Qualitative Checklist, and confidence of the findings was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation and Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research. title: Interprofessional Education Improves Understanding of Aspiration Pneumonia Risk Factors and Interprofessional Competence Among Dental Hygiene and Speech-Language Pathology Students
abstract: Purpose: Poor oral health and oropharyngeal dysphagia are modifiable risk factors for aspiration pneumonia. Dental hygienists (DHs) and speech-language pathologists (SLP) provide specialized services to individuals with these issues and may benefit from interdisciplinary knowledge in these areas. The objective of this study was to assess how an interprofessional education (IPE) event influenced students' knowledge and competence in working with individuals at risk for aspiration pneumonia. Method: The current study was a prospective, within-subjects cohort design. Participants included speech-language pathology and dental hygiene students ( N = 52). The 3-hr IPE event provided didactic and hands-on training that focused on the modifiable risk factors for aspiration pneumonia. Outcomes were assessed with a content assessment, the Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) Competency Self-Assessment Tool (Version 3), the Interprofessional Attitudes Scale (IPAS), and written feedback. title: Upward Effortful Pitch Glide as a Predictor of Pharyngeal Constriction in Individuals With Upper Versus Lower Motor Neuron Lesions
abstract: Purpose: This study tested the validity of using nasoendoscopy ratings of volitional maximum pharyngeal constriction (PCmax) during nasoendoscopy recordings of effortful upward pitch glide to predict pharyngeal area at maximum constriction (PAM) during swallowing recordings (VFSSs) in individuals with upper motor neuron (UMN) versus lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions. Method: Retrospective analysis of electronic medical records identified individuals with UMN or LMN lesions who underwent both VFSS and nasoendoscopy within 3 months. Blinded expert judges rated the degree and symmetry of PCmax in paired nasoendoscopic images of quiet breathing (minimum pharyngeal constriction) and highest pitch production (PCmax). Sixty-five percent of paired images were rated twice for intra- and interrater reliability estimates of agreement; consensus-based ratings were used when disagreement occurred. Comparisons between PCmax ratings and dichotomized VFSS PAM measures from 3-cc and 20-cc liquid bolus trials within UMN and LMN groups were assessed using univariate logistic regression. title: The Impact of Hospitals on Language Learning: A Case Study of a 3-Year-Old Boy With Developmental Delay Who Needed Augmentative and Alternative Communication
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this pilot study was to describe the language learning contexts experienced by a young child with global developmental delays and limited speech during an inpatient stay. Method: An observational case study was completed to describe the language learning contexts during the inpatient stay of a 3-year-old child with global developmental delay. Six health care providers participated and interacted with him during the 16-hr observational period over two consecutive days. Interactions were video-recorded and coded, and researcher memos were used to describe environmental variables. Results: During the observation period, the child interacted with at least one adult partner for a total of 6 hr. During the remaining 10 hr, he did not have human contact. His stay was characterized by extended periods without adult interaction interspersed with concentrated periods of linguistic input by providers during activities related to medical procedures, mealtimes, daily care, and therapy sessions. Providers were generally unfamiliar with his signals, preferences, and routine. They demonstrated general responsiveness during caregiving activities and positive affect during mo

title: Response to the Letters by Chang and Bernstein Ratner
abstract: Purpose: In our original article, we draw attention to the lifetime quality-of-life impairment that can result from childhood stuttering—hence, the need for immediate intervention after onset. We drew on existing experimental outcomes that parent speech-rate reduction and increased interturn speaker latency may reduce stuttering. We developed a two-factor treatment protocol based on those variables in combination and showed its clinical viability, suggesting that it would be a suitable target for Phase I–IV clinical trials. Chang and Bernstein Ratner wrote letters to the editor on our article, to which we respond. Conclusions: Our response to these letters to the editor covers the following issues raised by Chang and Bernstein Ratner: mechanisms of action for the proposed treatment, the evidence base for the treatment, plans to explore its treatment effects, and the need to verify its safety.

title: Variability of Preschool Stuttering During a Day
abstract: Purpose: Severity ratings (SRs) of children's stuttering assigned by parents and speech-language pathologists (SLPs) have advantages over methods based on stuttering counts. They are valid, simple, and convenient; without cost; and can be used without the child's awareness. The aim of this project was to study, for the first time, the use of an SR scale by parents and SLPs to track stuttering severity for preschool children over a typical day. For that purpose, we used 10 case studies. Method: Participants were 10 preschool children who stuttered (3–4 years of age) and their parents. Each child's speech was audio-recorded by their parent for an entire day at home, commencing at approximately 8:00 a.m. During that day, an SLP made a randomly timed phone call, during which a 10-min sample of the child's speech was audio-recorded. At the end of the day, both before and after training in the use of a 10-point scale, parents assigned a “typical” SR score for their child's speech for the day. title: Narrative Tell and Retell in Mandarin–English Bilingual Children
abstract: Purpose: Speech-language pathologists often adopt narrative tasks to assess bilingual children's language skills. However, limited research guides clinical decisions about elicitation method, assessment language, and interpretation of results for specific bilingual populations. The present study examined the impact of elicitation method (tell vs. retell) and language (Mandarin vs. English) on macro- and microstructure narrative skills in Mandarin–English bilingual children. Method: We collected narrative tell and retell samples from 79 Mandarin–English bilingual children using the Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives both online and in-person and analyzed macro- and microstructure measures in each language. Results: For macrostructure, children produced better narrative retells than tells across story structure, story complexity, and number of internal state terms, with cross-linguistic differences only in story structure (Mandarin > English). Code-switching did not significantly impact macrostructure scores. title: Developing a Clinically Practical Tool to Evaluate Directed Caregiver Communication in Early Intervention: A Pilot Study of the Tool's Reliability and Validity
abstract: Purpose: Early intervention (EI) relies heavily on directed caregiver communication (DCC), yet most clinical tools focus primarily on the child. This pilot study examined the reliability and validity of the Directed Caregiver Communication Assessment Tool (DCC-AT), which was developed by the authors to describe caregiver communication during naturalistic caregiver–child interactions. Method: This study used secondary data from the Early Communication Indicator for Autism (ECI-A), a naturalistic, 6-min play-based assessment during caregiver–child interaction. Participants included 10 autistic and 10 non-autistic children, all 36 months of age or younger, with test–retest videos for the autistic group resulting in 30 ECI-A videos. Coders used the DCC-AT to assess the types and frequencies of DCC strategies across four primary categories using partial interval coding. Result: Analyses showed that the DCC-AT captured observed variation in DCC and demonstrated strong interrater reliability. title: Comparing Traditional Motor Speech Practice to Contextualized Speech Practice in Preschoolers With Childhood Apraxia of Speech
abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study was to compare retention of real-word targets across practice conditions (contextualized vs. motor-only) within a modified integral stimulation treatment for preschoolers with childhood apraxia of speech (CAS). Method: A single-subject experimental design with alternating treatments was used with matched target sets randomly assigned to contextualized practice, motor-only practice, or no treatment. Three preschoolers with CAS completed 18 therapy sessions, each consisting of two 25-min blocks: one contextualized practice and one motor-only practice. Order of practice was randomized each visit. Changes in percent phonemes correct (PPC) and lexical stress accuracy, derived from blinded transcription, were explored with visual analysis and effect sizes (standardized mean difference, d statistic). Results: Meaningful improvements ( d > 1) were observed in PPC across words treated in contextualized practice for all three children immediately posttreatment and for two of three children at the 1-month follow-up. title: Speech-Language Pathologists' Confidence and Preparedness Working With Clients With Hearing Loss
abstract: Purpose: The primary purpose of this study was to assess the confidence and preparedness of speech-language pathologists (SLPs) to work with clients with hearing loss across various employment settings. Method: An online Qualtrics survey was used to collect data from respondents currently practicing in the United States and holding the Certificate of Clinical Competence in Speech-Language Pathology. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Multiple linear regressions were employed to assess the relation between confidence level and employment setting. Results: Sixty participants were included in the final analysis. Participants were most confident in checking to make sure devices (i.e., hearing aids, cochlear implants) were on. Working in a hospital setting was associated with higher confidence in working with hearing aids, while working in school settings was associated with lower confidence. Most participants indicated that they were mostly or very confident working with clients with hearing loss, with participants who worked in skilled nursing facilities associated with higher confidence. title: Paired-Comparison Versus Cross-Sectional Approaches for Assessing Longitudinal Speech Change in Parkinson's Disease Following Deep Brain Stimulation of the Subthalamic Nucleus
abstract: Purpose: Longitudinal changes in perceptual speech outcomes are typically derived from independent judgments at each time point rather than side by side within-speaker comparisons. This study evaluated a paired-comparison method for detecting longitudinal speech change in Parkinson's disease (PD) across three perceptual constructs (intelligibility, listener effort, and severity) relative to a cross-sectional method for detecting speech changes in the same cohort. Method: We collected recordings of the Speech Intelligibility Test at a baseline session and 12-month follow-up from speakers with PD after undergoing subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation implantation surgery and speakers with PD undergoing best medical management. Blinded naive listeners heard the recordings and provided cross-sectional judgments of intelligibility, listener effort, and speech severity. Another set of crowdsourced naive listeners completed a blinded online paired-comparison paradigm and judged changes in the same three constructs between baseline and 12-month sessions. We compared the sensitivity of paired-comparison measures to analogous cross-sectional measures for detecting 12-month speech change

title: Progression of Dysarthria, Drooling, and Swallowing Disorders in Parkinson's Disease: A 1-Year Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: Purpose: Dysarthria, drooling, and swallowing disorders are common motor problems in people with Parkinson's disease (PwP), leading to significant physical, emotional, and functional impairments that compromise quality of life. However, evidence on the progression of these disorders and their relationship with other features of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains scarce. This study aimed to investigate the progression of dysarthria, drooling, and swallowing disorders in PwP and identify predictors of progression. Method: A 1-year prospective cohort study was conducted with 73 PwP. Dysarthria was assessed using the Frenchay Dysarthria Assessment–Second Edition (FDA-2), drooling with Item 2.2 (Saliva and drooling) of the Movement Disorder Society–Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS), and swallowing with the Swallowing Clinical Assessment Score in Parkinson's Disease (SCAS-PD). The FDA-2 and SCAS-PD rely on clinician assessment, whereas MDS-UPDRS Item 2.2 (Saliva and drooling) assesses patient-reported problems with saliva control. title: Caregiver-Implemented Early Language Interventions for Latine Children With Language Delays: A Systematic Review
abstract: Purpose: Empowering caregivers with tools to support their children with language delays can potentially increase access to services for families from diverse backgrounds. The purpose of this systematic review was to describe the outcomes and characteristics of caregiver-implemented early language interventions studied or implemented with Spanish-speaking or bilingual Latine children with language delays. We also examined the extent to which these interventions were culturally and linguistically adapted. Method: Six search engines were used to identify articles published between 1990 and 2024. We completed a hand search of reference lists within eligible articles. We completed data extraction with an emphasis on the intervention's characteristics, outcomes for caregivers and children, and cultural and linguistic adaptations. Results: Ten articles were included in this review. Eight caregiver-implemented early language interventions have been studied with Latine children aged 18–47 months from Spanish-speaking families who exhibit language delays. title: Social Isolation in Adults Who Stutter: A Mixed-Methods Investigation of Risk and Correlates
abstract: Purpose: Social isolation is a commonly reported aspect of the stuttering experience. This study qualitatively explored adult stutterers' reports of social isolation while quantitatively examining possible correlates underlying the occurrence of social isolation in this population. Method: A sample of 264 adults who stutter were asked to share their experiences of social isolation and to complete measures of personality, stuttering role identity, social disconnectedness, and perceived isolation via an internet survey. Qualitative data were analyzed via thematic content analysis. Quantitative data were analyzed via linear and ordinal logistic regression to determine the influence of various correlates on social isolation. Results: Qualitative data indicated that the experience of social isolation is common to the experience of living as an adult who stutters. Responses indicated that social isolation in adults who stutter is influenced by personality differences, environmental components, and life experiences.
